pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Conservation of Mass

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry & Physics 'Matter'):** Conservation of mass in changes of state and chemical reactions; conservation of material and of mass, and reversibility, in melting, freezing, evaporation, sublimation, condensation and dissolving. (Bridged from KS2 change work.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-PS1-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-2] (heating, cooling, mixing, dissolving), the total weight of matter is conserved.

- **Operational details:** The principle: matter is neither created nor destroyed in a physical or chemical change — the TOTAL mass of a closed system is the same before and after. Teach it as a MEASURED law: weigh the whole system before and after a change (dissolve, mix, melt) and read the unchanged balance. The particle model supplies the WHY (the same particles are still there, just rearranged), which is why this sits just after 'matter is made of particles'. The hardest case is a change where something seems to vanish or appear: dissolved sugar (invisible but still weighed), and — as a bridge to reactions — a gas produced or consumed (mass only appears lost because gas escaped an OPEN container; seal it and mass holds). Stress 'account for the WHOLE system, including any gas'. Keep chemical-reaction conservation light at this age; the water-and-dissolving cases are the core.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal, quantitative). The child predicts and confirms that total mass is unchanged across a change, explains a 'disappearing' case (dissolved solid; escaped gas) by appeal to the whole system and to particles not being destroyed.
bestPractices: Teach conservation as a MEASURED law: weigh the whole system before and after and read the unchanged balance.
Use the particle model to supply the WHY — the same particles persist, only rearranged.
Confront the apparent-loss cases directly: dissolved solid (invisible but weighed) and gas escaping an OPEN container.
Resolve the open-container case by SEALING the system so the gas is counted.
Insist pupils account for the whole system, including any gas produced or absorbed.
keyRepresentations: A balance with before/after readouts on a sealed system
An open-vs-sealed toggle for a gas-producing reaction
A particle overlay showing the same particles rearranged, none destroyed
commonMisconceptions: Mass is lost when a solid dissolves because you can't see it.
Mass is destroyed when a gas is given off (forgetting the escaped gas has mass).
Burning destroys matter, so the ash weighs the same as nothing was added.
A change that makes something look bigger/smaller must change the mass.
Mass and volume are the same thing (a puffed-up product must weigh more).

learn.summary: For ages 10–11, investigate conservation of mass by accounting for a whole system before and after a change. A covered dissolving investigation and a sealed melting-ice investigation can provide real measurements for mixing and for a change of state caused by heating or cooling; prepared experimental data or a clearly labelled model can extend the comparison to gas-producing reactions in open and closed systems. In physical changes the material is still present; in chemical reactions atoms are rearranged into different substances rather than created or destroyed. Distinguish conserved mass from a balance reading affected by escaping matter, leaks, evaporation, condensation on the outside of a cold container, instrument precision or changing air buoyancy. Keep the chemical-reaction explanation introductory.

activities.title: Mass detective: track the whole system
feedback: If a learner expects dissolved sugar to become weightless, connect the before/after readings to the material remaining in solution. Readings that agree within measurement precision support that account.

If the open reaction seems to violate conservation, identify the gas that left the weighed system. A decrease can reflect escaped gas, but do not claim every change in reading is exactly the gas mass without considering other losses and measurement effects.

If the learner says nothing changed, distinguish appearance from substance: sugar dispersed during dissolving; a chemical reaction forms new substances by rearranging atoms. Neither requires matter to disappear.

For an expanding balloon or bag, explain that greater displaced air increases the upward buoyant force, so an unchanged total mass need not produce an exactly unchanged apparent balance reading. Do not respond by sealing the reaction in an improvised rigid pressure vessel.

Always identify the whole system and what crosses its boundary. Any real gas-producing demonstration must follow an established, supervised school protocol and an appropriate risk assessment; otherwise use prepared data or a model.
activities.rationale: A before/after dissolving measurement lets learners generate evidence while tracking material that becomes invisible. Prepared gas-reaction data can contrast open and closed boundaries without requiring an improvised pressurised experiment. A labelled model or particle overlay may support explanation, but its conserved total follows from its design and is not independent experimental proof. These are proposed activities, not validated interventions.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3: conservation of mass in changes of state and chemical reactions; conservation of material and mass and reversibility in melting/freezing/evaporation/sublimation/condensation/dissolving
NGSS 5-PS1-2: measure and graph to show total weight of matter is conserved regardless of change type (heating/cooling/mixing/dissolving)
Students think mass is lost when a gas escapes an open container or when a solid dissolves; sealing the system and accounting for gas resolves it
learnerActions: Place water and sugar, initially separate but both inside the same covered container, on a balance and record the whole-system reading.
Without adding or removing material, mix until the sugar dissolves. Reweigh the covered container in the same position, allowing any movement of the balance to settle.

Compare the readings within the balance’s resolution and explain why invisible dissolved sugar is still present. If readings differ, consider spills, evaporation, material left outside the weighed system or measurement variation before drawing a conclusion.

Use a particle picture or optional overlay to show sugar particles dispersed through the water rather than destroyed. Then test a change of state: weigh an ice cube sealed in a bag or covered container, let it melt at room temperature, wipe off any condensation that forms on the outside, and reweigh. Explain why the water's mass stays the same within the balance's resolution even though its state changed.
Use prepared experimental observations or a labelled model of an open vinegar-and-bicarbonate reaction. Predict what happens as gas leaves the weighed system, then inspect the data or model output.

Compare with prepared data or a model of a closed system that retains the gas. An optional flexible bag or flask-with-balloon illustration shows how gas can remain within the system; it is not a home procedure for sealing a gas-producing reaction in a rigid vessel.

Explain the distinction: total mass is conserved when all material is included, while a measured balance reading may change if matter escapes or if the apparatus expands and displaces more air. A model illustrates its built-in assumptions rather than supplying new experimental evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Dissolved material retains its mass. Chemical reactions rearrange atoms into products, including gases, without destroying the atoms. A closed system retains the material; an open weighed container can lose material as gas leaves. Balance readings must be interpreted with the measurement conditions.

activities.title: Consolidate: where did the mass go?
feedback: If the learner cannot say where material went, identify it explicitly: dissolved sugar remains in the liquid; escaped gas has left the weighed container; trapped gas remains part of a closed system.

A worked diagram can support explanation and review. Ask the learner to interpret fresh measurements or data too, and distinguish a schematic constant mass from a claim that every real balance reading must be identical.
activities.rationale: A before/after diagram with optional explanation flaps offers a worked example and a chance to compare the learner’s account with a material-tracking explanation. It does not establish an experimental result by itself; this is a proposed companion to measurements or prepared data.
learnerActions: Study before/after measurement data or diagrams for dissolving and open-versus-closed gas-producing reactions. Identify whether each display represents real measurements, idealised data or a model.
Reveal a 'where did the mass go?' explanation flap and check it against your own reasoning.

For the open reaction, explain why escaping gas can lower the reading. State which material must be included in a closed-system comparison, and why a flexible expanding apparatus can complicate the balance reading.
Account for every bit of matter in the change by naming where it ended up (in solution, as trapped gas, etc.).
activities.intendedInsight: Conservation requires accounting for material and system boundaries. Invisible dissolved material remains present, and gas has mass; apparent measurement changes need an explanation based on what was weighed and how it was measured.

activities.title: Predict and justify the balance reading
feedback: If the numerical prediction has a weak reason, ask which material is where and whether gas remains inside the system.

If a learner predicts less total mass in the closed model, ask where any atoms would have gone. If they predict a small decrease in a real expanding-balloon balance reading, discuss buoyancy and measurement effects instead of automatically marking it wrong.

Require an explanation for an open-system decrease that tracks escaping matter rather than claiming that gas disappears or has no mass. Consider additional measurement effects if the data require them.
activities.rationale: Prediction plus explanation can reveal whether a learner tracks material and distinguishes the system from its measured reading. Compare predictions with actual dissolving measurements or prepared gas-reaction data; model output is a conditional illustration. No effectiveness claim is established for this task design.
sourceClaims: NGSS 5-PS1-2: measure and graph to show total weight of matter is conserved regardless of change type (heating/cooling/mixing/dissolving)
learnerActions: Before revealing the data, predict the total mass for a closed dissolving system and an idealised closed gas-reaction model. Separately predict what a real balance might show, noting measurement precision and whether the apparatus expands.
Choose, from options, the correct explanation for why an OPEN fizzing reaction appears to lose mass.
Justify each prediction by naming the system boundary, the material present and any material that can leave. For a chemical reaction, refer to atoms rearranging into new products, including gas.
activities.intendedInsight: A useful prediction distinguishes conserved total mass from an instrument reading and is supported by tracking material, including gas, rather than by reciting a slogan.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: compare open and closed system data
feedback: If the learner says the wax or tablet is used up and gone, distinguish a starting substance being consumed from its atoms disappearing. Trace those atoms into products, and include oxygen entering a combustion system.

If the learner says gas has no mass, use reliable prepared measurements or an appropriate established classroom demonstration to show that gases contribute mass. Avoid treating inflation of a flexible balloon as a direct mass measurement without considering displaced air.

If the learner thinks dissolved sugar adds no mass, account for the known sugar added to the same initial water amount and check for spills or evaporation. The dissolved material remains in the system.

A full explanation predicts conserved total mass for a closed system, traces atoms into products, tracks escaped gas in an open system, and separates the principle from measurement artefacts. For physical dissolving, the sugar disperses rather than vanishing.
activities.rationale: The contrast between a recited conservation rule and an explanation that tracks atoms, products and boundaries can be explored through prediction and data interpretation. The candle and dissolving extensions test transfer to different changes. Real measurements, idealised data and model outputs must be identified separately; these proposals have not been empirically validated.
sourceClaims: Students think mass is lost when a gas escapes an open container or when a solid dissolves; sealing the system and accounting for gas resolves it
learnerActions: Use a prepared measurement record of an effervescent tablet reacting with water in an open vessel. Before viewing the later readings, predict their trend and explain where the produced gas can go.
Compare with prepared data from an established supervised closed-system protocol, or use a clearly labelled idealised model. Do not improvise a stopper-on rigid-flask reaction.

Observe the records or model outputs. For a closed system, explain conserved total mass; if real readings differ, inspect the apparatus, expansion, possible leakage and measurement precision instead of assuming matter was destroyed.

Use a flexible-bag or flask-with-balloon illustration to explain that retaining gas accounts for the material. Label expansion and its possible buoyancy effect on the balance; no exact unchanged reading is guaranteed.

Transfer the explanation to a diagram of a candle burning: identify oxygen entering and gaseous products leaving an open system, rather than treating wax alone as the whole system. Explain why a sealed-jar scenario differs without performing a sealed combustion experiment.
For water and sugar, compare equal initial water amounts before and after adding a known sugar mass without losing material. Explain why dissolved sugar adds mass even though it is no longer visible.
activities.intendedInsight: Atoms persist through the chemical reactions and are rearranged into products: an effervescent reaction produces gas and dissolved products; wax burning consumes oxygen and produces gases. The total mass of all inputs and outputs is conserved. Open-vessel readings omit escaping material, while closed-system readings still require attention to measurement conditions.

constraints: Target age 10–11; keep chemical-reaction conservation light — water, dissolving, and a simple gas-producing reaction are the core cases.
Always require learners to account for the WHOLE system, including any gas produced or absorbed; this is the crux that resolves the apparent-loss cases.

Distinguish the changes accurately: combustion (wax burning) is not the same as an effervescent tablet reacting in water; both conserve mass but by different reactions, so do not label the fizzing tablet as 'burnt'.

Do not improvise a sealed rigid-vessel gas-producing reaction. Use prepared data or a clearly labelled model for the closed-gas comparison unless an adult is following an established supervised school protocol with appropriate apparatus and risk assessment. A flexible bag or balloon can illustrate gas retention, but expansion changes air buoyancy and can alter the apparent balance reading.

Worked diagrams, explanation flaps, data tables and models may support interpretation. Distinguish their stated or built-in results from measurements the learner makes; no single format is a necessary first teaching method.
Predict-only or recognition-only responses do not show whether a learner can trace the matter through the change; require an explanation that names where the matter went.

Ask for an account of the material and system boundary, not just a slogan. Distinguish physical changes, in which material can disperse or change state, from chemical changes, in which atoms rearrange into different substances.

Interpret observations within instrument resolution and experimental conditions. Total mass conservation does not require an identical balance display when a flexible container expands, gas leaks, material evaporates, or temperature and air currents affect the reading.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The saved research used categorical medium preferences. This guidance retains distinct affordances—physical measurements, worked diagrams, prediction checks and optional models—without claiming that one format is necessary or that these activities are proven effective.
The original claim that a sim 'delivers the law and its key caveat' and similar strong efficacy wording has not been empirically established by the cited sources; retained as proposals only.
One source ('Students think mass is lost...' ACS/RSC guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as unverified in any downstream use.

Editorial repair distinguishes conserved mass from a changing apparent balance reading, atoms from molecules in chemical reactions, and physical observations from built-in model results. Gas-reaction comparisons use prepared data or a model unless an established supervised protocol is available.

The factual audit correctly raised the buoyancy effect of expanding flexible apparatus, but its proposed capped-bottle procedure was not adopted. This guidance removes improvised sealed rigid gas-reaction instructions and exact-reading guarantees. No fresh source verification was performed.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: put a fizzing tablet and water in a flask, first with the stopper OFF, then a fresh one with the stopper ON, each on a balance. Ask the child to predict each reading over time and WHY. A 'matter destroyed / gas weightless' model predicts a drop in both. Open drops (gas escapes); sealed stays constant. The pre-observation reasoning is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If I did the SAME candle burning in the OPEN air on the balance, would the reading change? Why is that different from the sealed jar?
The wax turned into gas — does that gas weigh anything? How could we prove it?
Dissolve sugar until it vanishes: is the beaker heavier, lighter, or the same? Why?
If matter is never destroyed, where exactly did every bit of the wax end up?
assess.correctAnswer: In the SEALED jar the total reading stays the SAME: matter isn't destroyed — the wax turns into gases (carbon dioxide and water vapour) that are still inside the jar, so the total mass is conserved. The reason must invoke 'the gas is still there and has mass', not just 'nothing changed'.

errorPatterns.pattern: burning destroys matter, so mass is lost ('the wax is used up and gone')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Track the atoms: wax + oxygen → CO2 + water vapour, all still in the sealed jar. Weigh a sealed reaction to show no drop. Confront the 'used up' idea directly.
errorPatterns.distractor: It goes down, because the wax is burnt away and gone.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts the reading drops; can't say where the wax went

errorPatterns.pattern: gases have no mass / weigh nothing ('it's only gas now, so it weighs less')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Weigh a sealed syringe/flask of gas vs vacuum, or an inflated vs deflated ball — gas has mass. Then re-run the conservation argument.
errorPatterns.distractor: It goes down, because gas doesn't weigh anything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: accepts gas forms but says gas is weightless, so predicts a drop

errorPatterns.pattern: dissolved solid stops contributing to weight because you can't see it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Weigh water, add sugar, weigh again — heavier by the sugar. Invisible isn't weightless; link back to dissolving conservation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: for the dissolving case, says sugar-water weighs the same as plain water

responseLevels.gap: Predicts a change in the sealed jar because matter is destroyed or gas is weightless; can't track where the wax went.
responseLevels.full: Predicts 'same' in the sealed jar AND explains by tracking matter (wax→gases still present, gases have mass), correctly distinguishes the open system (gas leaves), and applies conservation to dissolving — invisible is not weightless.
responseLevels.partial: States 'mass is conserved / matter isn't destroyed' and predicts 'same' for the sealed jar, but can't explain the OPEN-air case (gas escapes) or apply conservation to dissolving — the principle is recited, not traced through the matter.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I weigh a lit candle sitting on a balance in a sealed jar. As it burns, wax disappears. Does the reading on the balance go down, up, or stay the same while it burns in the sealed jar? Then the key part: explain WHY, using where the matter goes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason distinguishes a child who tracks matter through the change (wax→invisible gases that still weigh something, trapped in the jar) from one who believes burning/dissolving destroys matter or that gases are weightless. The sealed jar is chosen precisely so a 'matter is destroyed' model predicts a DROP.
